name: table-count
description: Number of Drizzle pgTable() definitions across shared/. The mature-machine north star is a SMALLER schema (<=450 tables); today's count is far above it. This strict down-only ratchet makes the schema monotonic: adding a table fails CI until the baseline is deliberately bumped (a conscious 'yes we need this'), and every consolidation lowers the baseline toward the target. Founder-chosen 'strict' 2026-07-16.
lastBumpNote: 761 -> 763 on 2026-08-13: va_tasks + va_sops -- the VA subsystem's persistence layer, built on an explicit founder ruling (BLOCKERS B9; the founder's picker answer names 'real tables + migration for VA tasks and the SOP library, wired to the existing routes'). That ruling IS the conscious 'yes we need this' this ratchet asks for. WHAT WAS THERE: services/vaManagement.ts declared its storage as two string constants -- VA_TASKS_KEY and SOP_LIBRARY_KEY -- and never read either. createTask was a PURE FUNCTION that stamped an id onto its input and returned it, so POST /api/va/tasks answered 200 with a record that existed only in that response; /api/va/metrics and /api/va/audit-trail computed over organizations.settings.va_tasks, an array with NO CREATOR anywhere in the repository, and returned zeros that READ AS MEASUREMENTS; POST /api/va/tasks/:id/verify read-modify-wrote that same array and could never find a task in it. NOT THE SETTINGS BLOB IT WAS AIMED AT: that column is read on nearly every org-scoped request, so an unbounded task history there grows the hot path for every user forever, and concurrent writers clobber each other -- the verify handler already carried a comment recording that exact bug being fixed once with jsonb_set. TWO TABLES AND NOT ONE: DEFAULT_SOPS stays a code constant (AcreOS's own procedure catalogue, versioned with the code that references it); va_sops holds what an ORG writes. Merging them would make a code change look like a customer edit. NOT DEFERRED TO A JSONB COLUMN ON organizations: tasks are a queryable, filterable, paginated collection with per-row lifecycle and per-row verification -- the thing a table is. Both are wired on arrival: GET/POST /api/va/tasks, GET /api/va/tasks/:id, PUT /api/va/tasks/:id, GET/POST /api/va/sops, plus the three existing read routes now reading the table. Recurring tasks were deliberately NOT built -- a schedule table with no runner would be the built-but-unwired defect this repo keeps finding, so GET /api/va/scheduled refuses with 501 instead. PRIOR NOTE -- 760 -> 761 on 2026-08-12: outcomes -- the learning layer, closing the canonical loop (BI1, AA8, canonical law 9). decision_snapshots froze what was KNOWN and PREDICTED and scenarios froze the ARITHMETIC; nothing recorded what the world then DID, so an investor's own history was a pile of forecasts nobody ever graded. AA8 names the Decision->Outcome graph as a compounding moat precisely because a competitor can copy a screen but not a customer's calibration. VARIANCE IS NOT A COLUMN: it is computed as a pure projection over the scenario references the decision already froze, because a stored variance is a third number that can drift from the two it derives from, and improving it later would silently restate how good a past decision looked. decision_snapshot_id IS a real foreign key, unlike the deliberately unconstrained subject_id on evidence_claims / decision_snapshots / scenarios -- those must SURVIVE their subject, whereas an outcome without its decision is meaningless: there is nothing to compare it against and nothing it can teach. The FK is correct here for exactly the reason it was wrong there. NOT REUSING outcome_telemetry (shaped around AGENT performance -- agentActions, messagesSent, responseTime -- and carrying no decision reference) or outcome_calibrations (keyed by agent codename): both are the agent/founder learning loop, and BI76 is explicit that these are different things that must not collapse into one log. BI178 is honoured in the projection: an outcome is an OBSERVATION of what happened, not retroactive validation of the decision, so describeVariance never says a decision was good or wrong -- a record that scores decisions by their results teaches an investor to be lucky rather than right.
